prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B025 as my single-part preference, and my confidence is somewhat higher than in round 1 because the discussion has narrowed the real dispute. Four members prefer it with identical names, and Danielsson, Eriksson, Olsson and Mehlig list it as acceptable or as a fallback, so it is the broadest common ground without anyone having to pretend that counts settle the science. The scientific core is a single clear idea: trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels on the clock transition, which removes Doppler and recoil limits while keeping a large atom number for stability. Katori proposed it and Ye's group took it to the 10^-18 regime and into many-body clock physics. Several national laboratories now reproduce this accuracy and compare clocks against each other, which is the robustness test I care about most. As a theorist working with superconducting-circuit experiments I also value that the clock opens measurable physics, such as millimetre-to-centimetre relativistic redshift tests, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter searches, and not only a better instrument. The topic is far from the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, and the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The chair is right that the case against B025 has not yet been answered in the ballots. Optical clocks can be read as metrology and capability rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and Mehlig, Danielsson and Olsson press this. The adjacent 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize overlap in community and tools, and Ye's clocks depend on the comb. My honest view is that a lattice clock at 10^-18 is a new regime of measurement, not a new fact about nature, so the prize would be an invention-type award, and I would not claim otherwise. The priority record for Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups is unchecked by me, and I rely on Lindroth and Kroll on atomic details. If the expert reports show that the first convincing Sr lattice clock demonstration belongs to someone outside Katori and Ye, the two names would need to change. B036 is the strongest alternative on my reading, because it is a discovery with a clean theory and experiment chain, but the omission of Bernevig and Hughes is a real problem that I cannot resolve with my expertise.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether lattice clocks are a physics discovery or a technology, and he and Eriksson argue that B036 is the cleaner discovery, with the Z2 class not covered by the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I take the technology objection seriously and I cannot fully dismiss it. Where I disagree is that the physics is separable from the instrument here: magic-wavelength cancellation is a statement about the atomic polarisability of two states, and its consequences, relativistic redshift across millimetres and constraints on constants, are measured physics. I also take his point about B036: the Z2 class is distinct from the 2016 work, and it is the case where nature gave the surprise. My difficulty is the credit chain you describe yourself. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang, who predicted the HgTe effect that was measured, and I would not be comfortable defending that in a citation. For B025 the credit gap is smaller and concerns priority, not a missing theory partner. That asymmetry is why I keep B025 first and B036 as the alternative.

responses.point: Olsson makes her B008 position conditional on whether the TEM and STEM corrector work is one invention or two, and says she would move to B025 if the priority of the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration is confirmed.
responses.response: I appreciate how openly you state the conditions for moving, and I think the B025 priority question is the right one to pin down. As I read the record, Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme in 2001-2003 and his group, with Takamoto, demonstrated the Sr lattice clock in 2005; this is the part I believe but have not verified, and I would ask Lindroth to confirm it. If so, Takamoto is best seen as a member of Katori's own group, which is how Kroll reads it, and Lemonde's contribution is to the clock's evaluation and a competing implementation. That would leave the two names unchanged. I defer to you on B008. A similar issue of two near-simultaneous correctors is exactly what makes my own two-name case look cleaner, but I would not use that against your colleagues' careful claim.

responses.point: Kroll discloses a mentor-lineage link between John Hall and Ye and leaves recusal to the Chair, and he proposes drawing the citation tightly to exclude the Th-229 nuclear clock and many-body clock work.
responses.response: I agree with both points. On conflict, I think disclosure is the right level for a lineage link that does not involve collaboration, funding or institutional ties. I would only ask the committee to record it. On the citation, I have kept my wording to the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, with magic-wavelength trapping named explicitly, because that separates it from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize and leaves the Th-229 nuclear clock for the future. I would also not name the many-body clock work, because it is a later development in Ye's group that is not yet needed to justify the prize.

responses.point: Lindroth says Takamoto, Lemonde and the early demonstrations have claims a two-name prize does not cover, and that Ye's group's contribution must be separated from the nuclear clock.
responses.response: I accept that a two-name prize does not cover every contribution, and the citation should not suggest it does. Before the final vote I would like your view on the one technical question I cannot judge as a non-specialist: whether the lattice light shift and blackbody radiation shift evaluations are robust enough, independent of the Ye group's own numbers, to support the 10^-18 claim in the citation. If you think the phrase should say 'near 10^-18' or refer to the accuracy that has been compared across laboratories, I would accept that wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept optical lattice clocks as a physics prize rather than as metrology close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. This is the main reason I do not hold my position with high confidence.

Priority of the first convincing Sr lattice-clock demonstration and how much credit Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups should receive; I have not verified this independently and rely on Lindroth and Kroll.
Whether B036 can be defended without Bernevig and Hughes, and whether the Z2 and HgTe citation is distinct enough from 2016; I cannot judge the condensed-matter credit chain.
Whether the exact 10^-18 wording in the citation is safe given that the best evaluations come from a small number of groups.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, so I should not drive any decision on B016 and, to a lesser degree, B009. B016 is no longer part of my preferred configuration or my alternatives. I have no connection to Katori, Ye or their groups, and none to B036 or B037. I note Kroll's mentor-lineage disclosure regarding Hall and Ye, and I think disclosure rather than recusal is sufficient. Kroll also mentions that our WACQT roles overlap institutionally, but that has no bearing on B025.
